Hot Soup

By: Harri Vithi | Commission

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
When billions are budgeted to feed the hungry… why are children still starving?

Unique Selling Point:
A government feeding scheme where it's unclear exactly where the food is and...who is really being fed.

Summary:
KwaZulu-Natal frequently records the highest number of child deaths due to malnutrition in the country.Recent Mortality Rates: Between April 2017 and April 2025, 555 children under the age of five died from moderate acute malnutrition in KZN public health facilities.
In the province, government is spending hundreds of millions to feed the poor. But on the ground, the food being served is raising serious questions. At the centre of our investigation is eThekwini’s soup kitchen programme — a system meant to feed thousands daily. Officially, the municipality says it’s spending around R141 million. But internal documents point to a R240 million figure

Further information:
And when we look closer at how that money is being spent — the numbers don’t add up.
In one case, a 10kg bag of samp is priced at R2000 — far above market value. Suppliers are paid through a complex panel system, where multiple companies are appointed, but exactly who supplies what — and at what cost — is difficult to trace.
Among them: companies with overlapping directorships… and others, like Msila Media, whose core bu siness - on the surface - appears far removed from feeding communities.
But this isn’t just about one programme.
Across the province, the cracks are widening.
In early childhood development centres — funded through a national budget of over R10 billion — delays in subsidy payments have forced some centres to scale back meals or shut their doors altogether. ECD centres have been forced to take the KZN government to court.
And in the school system, a R2.9 billion nutrition tender — feeding more than 2 million learners — is now facing legal challenges, with losing bidders alleging irregularities, newly registered companies being awarded contracts, and claims of political interference.
The department denies wrongdoing. But the questions remain. From ECD centres… to school feeding schemes… to municipal soup kitchens — billions are being spent in the name of fighting hunger.
And when the system meant to feed the most vulnerable begins to falter…
It’s not budgets that suffer. It’s people - it’s children. Hot Soup is an investigation into how a system designed to feed the hungry may be failing them — and what that failure looks like on the ground.


1. Interview: Lawrence Mngomezulu - Deputy Director of Friends of South Africa ECD Forum

Mngomezulu is the Deputy Chairperson of the Friends of South Africa Early Childhood Development (ECD) Forum and also runs his own ECD centre in KwaZulu-Natal.
The dual role is key: He is both an advocate at provincial level
And a practitioner on the ground, dealing directly with children and families

The Friends of South Africa ECD Forum is a network representing early childhood development centres across KwaZulu-Natal. nTheir work focuses on especially in low-income communities.
Advocating for government subsidies and funding ensuring young children receive:
daily meals, etc.
They sit at the frontline of child nutrition in poor communities

Recent developments in KZN show exactly many ECD centres have not been paid government subsidies on time. Some are owed months — even up to a year — of funding. Mngomezulu provides the “big picture” voice. He can explain:

why hunger in KZN is so widespread
how food insecurity affects children before they even reach school
how fragile the feeding system really is

Potential intro:

At the very start of a child’s life, before school, before formal systems — early childhood centres are often the first line of defence against hunger.

But according to Lawrence Mngomezulu from the Friends of South Africa ECD Forum, even that first line is beginning to crack.

Valuable for:
scale
impact
human reality

Key questions for him:
What are you seeing in terms of hunger among young children in KZN?
How dependent are children on meals provided at ECD centres?
What happens when subsidies don’t come through?
Are more children arriving hungry than before?
Are some families dependent on soup kitchens?

Interview 2: Family with young children (and Gogo) - areas Chatsworth, Burlington and Moriah
Soup kitchens operate between 10 a.m - 2 p.m on the ground
Councillor Rowena Bosman is canvassing Mount Moriah for families today.
Councillor Samantha Windvogel is canvassing Burlington
Founder Dawn Lappan - Thousand Hills says they’ll revert tomorrow with information on potential families we can screen (Outer Western Durban,, 30-40 kms out)
Renette Roskruge of Thabitha Foundation says she has families who would be more than willing to interview runs her soup kitchen on Thursday and Friday and will see what she can secure

Interview 3: EThekwini Municipality - to be informed of officials name. Committed to:-

Sit-down interview
Site visits of soup kitchens which we’ll select most problematic based on councillor on the-ground information

Two targeted companies:

Msila Media

Owned by Makhosazane Jennifer Sithole is listed at an RDP home which could very well be her family home - no problem Thing is Makhosazane appears to have dropped from the sky like a hot potato - registering Msila Media in 2020 but with no traceable work or business history before then. How did the 50+ woman survive - perhaps she was a housewife.

That’s plausible but perhaps she’s a domestic worker being used as a front but worse of all it’s Makhosazane’s company which lists 10kgs of samp for R 2000 - how did such bizarre pricing pass the eye of the municipality’s precise needle?

What’s we’ll do - Claire on the investigative trail - visit the home. Gve her a call and ask her where she operates her business rom but most importantly where she purchases her unique brand of samp for R 2000 for 10kgs.

Mavulizibusiso Enterprises/Davport Trading

The former lists two directors:

Palesa Gwala and Nombuso Nkosingiphile Mcanyana. Mcanyana does not sit in isolation—she is also a director of a second company, Zielungile.
Within Zielungile sits Zilungile Portia Nombelana, who is not just a linked name but the owner of Davport Trading.

That places Mcanyana and Nombelana one degree apart through a shared company structure.

Davport Trading, in turn, appears on the same tender award documentation as Mavulizibusiso Enterprises, bringing the two companies into the same procurement space. The overlap tightens further at a physical level: both Mavulizibusiso Enterprises and Davport Trading list the identical legal address—Umlazi Lodge, Block 23, Room 23, KwaZulu-Natal, 4066. One address, two companies, one tender environment, and a chain of directors that connects them step by step:

Mcanyana links Mavulizibusiso to Zielungile; Zielungile links to Nombelana; Nombelana leads to Davport.

Shoot dates: 20th and 21st April

Press Release:


Hot Soup
Dilapidated facilities, inflated prices and murky suppliers: government is spending hundreds of millions to feed the hungry, but the numbers just don’t add up. eThekwini’s soup kitchen programme is coming under scrutiny as images of unappetising food, uncollected waste, and rodent infestations make the rounds on social media. Meanwhile, documents reveal questionable suppliers charging above the odds for basic groceries, while government claims records have been faked. Where is the food, who is really being fed – and who is paying the price for a faltering system? Carte Blanche investigates.
Producer: Harri Vithi | Presenter: Masa Kekana

Script:


(Masa) These images are of soup kitchens run by the Ethekwini Municipality in KZN. They began circulating on social media just weeks ago: disintegrating kitchen floors, uncollected waste, a dilapidated room - used interchangeably as a toilet and for washing cooking equipment

(Community member) So,there’s a rat infestation here?

(Volunteer) Yes,rats.

(Masa) It's an unhealthy condition for even just cooking, never mind living. When last did you conduct a site visit there?

(Mndeni Mkhize) Well we were there, even yesterday, the program officers did pitch at the site.

(Masa) On the menu: this brown soup destined for vulnerable communities across the municipality.

(Masa)The Ethekwini Municipality, which incorporates Durban and surrounds, runs 94 soup kitchens which, on paper, provide a hot meal to the indigent. Every three years or so, it puts out a multi-million Rand tender for the supply of groceries, bread and gas. Last year, thirty companies tendered successfully.

(Masa) These documents, apparently published by the Municipality, put the current cost of the programme at R241 million over 3 years.

(Masa) This is one of Ethekwini Municipality’s soup kitchens - now as you can see from the entrance, the conditions are quite deplorable - where they’re supposed to be cooking a healthy nutritious meal

(Masa) Its state leaves us wondering what more than 240 million Rand is being spent on.

(Masa) And it seems our presence here is causing tension.

(Masa) Well so much for a nutritious meal, we arrived here and there were queues of people with empty bowls waiting to get some food. Well they left with their empty bowls but were given some sliced brown bread.

(Masa) As tensions rise, we’re forced to leave.

(Anonymous Source) People only receive bread - dry bread and go home with empty bowls. It's what I witness all the time.

(Masa) From a safer distance, a community source helps to explain the hostility.

(Anonymous Source) Once you speak out about what is the truth, now you become a target. You might be killed at any moment.

(Masa) But, why would speaking out on contracts to feed the poor lead to threats of violence? Our attempt to answer that question begins with the tender documents.

(Masa) This is the list of companies currently supplying anything from oxtail soup to dishwashing liquid. Crucially, it also lists the prices charged to the Municipality.

(Masa) As we go through procurement documents, one line stands out…

(Masa) A 10 kilogram bag of samp ..priced at two thousand rand.

(Masa) But samp at 20 times the going rate isn’t the biggest surprise revealed by these documents.

(Masa) That comes from closer inspection of one of the companies providing the samp; not a co-op, not a wholesaler but an entity called Msila Media.

(Masa) It has no online footprint. It's owned by a woman called Makhosazane Sithole and is registered to this address.

(Masa) We've just arrived at the listed address of Msila Media, the supplier linked to the R 2000 10 kilogram samp tender.

(Masa) Hello, I’m looking for Msila Media - Makhosazane Sithole?

(Masa) You don’t know her?

Masa) You know, ma’am. There’s a business registered under your address.

(Resident) Hayibo!

(Masa) Bizarrely, the people that live at this listed address know nothing about Msila Media, in fact, the woman says clearly there’s some kind of fraud going on.

(Masa) So we call Sithole for answers.

(Masa) We’d like to know how you registered this address that isn’t your business address - an RDP house in Lamontville?

(Makhosazane Sithole )As I said, please call me tomorrow so I can check.

(Masa) Your one business that gets a lot of money to feed the hungry from Ethekwini Municipality - you don’t know that business address?

(Makhosazane Sithole) I'm saying, wait for me while I look into my affairs.

(Masa) Let’s talk about the samp that you charge R 2000 for a 10 kilogram bag - why would you do that?

(Makhosazane Sithole) You know, when you have a business, you have employees.
So I need to get clarity on the questions you're asking me. That’s why I’m saying, I’ll get back to you tomorrow.

(Masa) Perhaps unsurprisingly, we never hear from Sithole again.

(Masa) Forty kilometers away, a non-profit organisation is quietly doing its part to fight the hunger crisis. Its work stands in stark contrast to what we saw in Ethekwini.

(Bigboy Hlongwa) On a daily basis usually we do about minimum 9000 plates of meals.
From 6 a.m in the morning as you will see they will utilize a hundred litre pots.

(Masa) And that’s with just one kitchen, which we’re shown by the charity’s Bigboy Hlongwa.

(Masa) Roughly, how much does it cost to feed everyone - the cost of a plate?

(Bigboy Hlongwa) Breakfast, you average about R 4.40 and then lunch it actually comes up to about R 7 plus for each plate and then obviously also including the snacks, might be even sometimes fruits - it averages about R 2, so in complete it’s around about R 13 odd.

(Masa) Children like Enzokuhle Ngcobo may face a school day on an empty stomach. Her grandmother, Buyisiwe, struggles to make ends meet.

(Buyisiwe Ngcobo) I live with my grandchildren. Their mother passed away when they were younger.
(Buyisiwe Ngcobo) I had three children. They all passed away.

(Masa) The family is completely reliant on 1000 Hills.

(Masa) And while a 1000 Hills survives on the support of sponsors, the Ethekwini Municipality has access to millions of taxpayer Rands. Mndeni Mkhize, works in the unit responsible for its feeding scheme.

(Masa) Does the municipality have a set guideline that it uses in terms of following nutritional diets?

(Mndeni Mkhize) Monday is bread day, so you get bread with macaroni and soup with soup bones or chicken feet and necks.

(Masa) What we saw were people with empty bowls, leaving with empty bowls, just being given dry sliced brown bread.

(Mndeni Mkhize) We'll have to investigate the matter and make sure that we hold whoever must be held responsible in terms of our normal procedures

(Masa) We wonder whether those investigations will extend to Msila Media.

(Masa) The listed address, this RDP home in Lamontville - the residents who live there say they know nothing about Msila Media. What due diligence was really done here?

(Mndeni Mkhize) We are going to precisely look into it and zoom into it to make sure that if anything went wrong then there are consequences for that particular action.

(Masa) The shocker for everyone is that Msila Media charged you as a municipality 2000 Rand for a 10 kilogram bag of samp.

(Masa) Mndeni, though, says the online documents are fake and the approved price was R 98

(Mndeni Mkhize) I don't know now with new technologies and people being able to edit, then a lot can happen.

(Masa) The Municipality says the value of the programme has also been exaggerated and is actually around R141 million.

(Masa) Surely you cannot have your volunteers cooking in a litter infested place that's got rodents all over?

(Mndeni Mkhize) I will not concede to say we’re preparing food in an infested environment and so forth

(Masa) I was there yesterday personally, it is dirty - it is filthy and if you don’t want to concede to that there’s a bigger problem.

(Mndeni Mkhize) I can assure you that the food that is being prepared is a food that can be consumed by the people that we are serving.

(Masa) Anyone serving food must have a Certificate of Acceptability - to verify safety standards have been met.

(Masa) Do you have certificates of acceptability for your soup kitchens?

(Mndeni Mkhize) Not certificates of acceptability per se, but we are relying on them. Our samples of food in soup kitchens also get tested.

(Masa) So they’re doing their work but you aren't getting the certificate.

(Mndeni Mkhize) Part of the problems they are raising, we are in the process of fixing. I think once those structures are there, then we will be able to be issued with those particular certificates.

(Masa) So it appears the soup kitchens aren’t legally compliant, but the municipality gives us access to pre-selected sites.

(Masa) So we’re at one of the soup kitchens that the municipality insisted that we come see.

(Masa) They’re not the sites we wanted to see but municipal officials have none-the-less arrived in numbers. They decline to answer questions on camera and can’t tell us how much a single meal costs.

(Masa) Then, out of nowhere, there’s shouting from one of the queues.

(Community Member) This is rubbish! We are dogs.

(Crowd) Hayibo!

(Community Member) The government says they’re giving us food, when they give us this?
Is it the mayor that’s giving us this s***? Are we that poor?

(Masa) While hundreds of millions are spent to feed the vulnerable, on the ground serious questions remain about what that money is really delivering.

(Masa)The Ethekwini Municipality, which incorporates Durban and surrounds, runs 94 soup kitchens which, on paper, provide a hot meal to the indigent. Every three years or so, it puts out a multi-million Rand tender for the supply of groceries, bread and gas. Last year, thirty companies tendered successfully. (Masa) These documents, apparently published by the Municipality, put the current cost of the programme at R241 million over 3 years. (Masa) This is one of Ethekwini Municipality’s soup kitchens - now as you can see from the entrance, the conditions are quite deplorable - where they’re supposed to be cooking a healthy nutritious meal (Masa) Its state leaves us wondering what more than 240 million Rand is being spent on. (Masa) And it seems our presence here is causing tension. (Masa) Well so much for a nutritious meal, we arrived here and there were queues of people with empty bowls waiting to get some food. Well they left with their empty bowls but were given some sliced brown bread. (Masa) As tensions rise, we’re forced to leave. (Anonymous Source) People only receive bread - dry bread and go home with empty bowls. It's what I witness all the time. (Masa) From a safer distance, a community source helps to explain the hostility. (Anonymous Source) Once you speak out about what is the truth, now you become a target. You might be killed at any moment. (Masa) But, why would speaking out on contracts to feed the poor lead to threats of violence? Our attempt to answer that question begins with the tender documents. (Masa) This is the list of companies currently supplying anything from oxtail soup to dishwashing liquid. Crucially, it also lists the prices charged to the Municipality. (Masa) As we go through procurement documents, one line stands out… (Masa) A 10 kilogram bag of samp ..priced at two thousand rand. (Masa) But samp at 20 times the going rate isn’t the biggest surprise revealed by these documents. (Masa) That comes from closer inspection of one of the companies providing the samp; not a co-op, not a wholesaler but an entity called Msila Media. (Masa) It has no online footprint. It's owned by a woman called Makhosazane Sithole and is registered to this address. (Masa) We've just arrived at the listed address of Msila Media, the supplier linked to the R 2000 10 kilogram samp tender. (Masa) Hello, I’m looking for Msila Media - Makhosazane Sithole? (Masa) You don’t know her? Masa) You know, ma’am. There’s a business registered under your address. (Resident) Hayibo! (Masa) Bizarrely, the people that live at this listed address know nothing about Msila Media, in fact, the woman says clearly there’s some kind of fraud going on. (Masa) So we call Sithole for answers. (Masa) We’d like to know how you registered this address that isn’t your business address - an RDP house in Lamontville? (Makhosazane Sithole )As I said, please call me tomorrow so I can check. (Masa) Your one business that gets a lot of money to feed the hungry from Ethekwini Municipality - you don’t know that business address? (Makhosazane Sithole) I'm saying, wait for me while I look into my affairs. (Masa) Let’s talk about the samp that you charge R 2000 for a 10 kilogram bag - why would you do that? (Makhosazane Sithole) You know, when you have a business, you have employees. So I need to get clarity on the questions you're asking me. That’s why I’m saying, I’ll get back to you tomorrow. (Masa) Perhaps unsurprisingly, we never hear from Sithole again. (Masa) Forty kilometers away, a non-profit organisation is quietly doing its part to fight the hunger crisis. Its work stands in stark contrast to what we saw in Ethekwini. (Bigboy Hlongwa) On a daily basis usually we do about minimum 9000 plates of meals. From 6 a.m in the morning as you will see they will utilize a hundred litre pots. (Masa) And that’s with just one kitchen, which we’re shown by the charity’s Bigboy Hlongwa. (Masa) Roughly, how much does it cost to feed everyone - the cost of a plate? (Bigboy Hlongwa) Breakfast, you average about R 4.40 and then lunch it actually comes up to about R 7 plus for each plate and then obviously also including the snacks, might be even sometimes fruits - it averages about R 2, so in complete it’s around about R 13 odd. (Masa) Children like Enzokuhle Ngcobo may face a school day on an empty stomach. Her grandmother, Buyisiwe, struggles to make ends meet. (Buyisiwe Ngcobo) I live with my grandchildren. Their mother passed away when they were younger. (Buyisiwe Ngcobo) I had three children. They all passed away. (Masa) The family is completely reliant on 1000 Hills. (Masa) And while a 1000 Hills survives on the support of sponsors, the Ethekwini Municipality has access to millions of taxpayer Rands. Mndeni Mkhize, works in the unit responsible for its feeding scheme. (Masa) Does the municipality have a set guideline that it uses in terms of following nutritional diets? (Mndeni Mkhize) Monday is bread day, so you get bread with macaroni and soup with soup bones or chicken feet and necks. (Masa) What we saw were people with empty bowls, leaving with empty bowls, just being given dry sliced brown bread. (Mndeni Mkhize) We'll have to investigate the matter and make sure that we hold whoever must be held responsible in terms of our normal procedures (Masa) We wonder whether those investigations will extend to Msila Media. (Masa) The listed address, this RDP home in Lamontville - the residents who live there say they know nothing about Msila Media. What due diligence was really done here? (Mndeni Mkhize) We are going to precisely look into it and zoom into it to make sure that if anything went wrong then there are consequences for that particular action. (Masa) The shocker for everyone is that Msila Media charged you as a municipality 2000 Rand for a 10 kilogram bag of samp. (Masa) Mndeni, though, says the online documents are fake and the approved price was R 98 (Mndeni Mkhize) I don't know now with new technologies and people being able to edit, then a lot can happen. (Masa) The Municipality says the value of the programme has also been exaggerated and is actually around R141 million. (Masa) Surely you cannot have your volunteers cooking in a litter infested place that's got rodents all over? (Mndeni Mkhize) I will not concede to say we’re preparing food in an infested environment and so forth (Masa) I was there yesterday personally, it is dirty - it is filthy and if you don’t want to concede to that there’s a bigger problem. (Mndeni Mkhize) I can assure you that the food that is being prepared is a food that can be consumed by the people that we are serving. (Masa) Anyone serving food must have a Certificate of Acceptability - to verify safety standards have been met. (Masa) Do you have certificates of acceptability for your soup kitchens? (Mndeni Mkhize) Not certificates of acceptability per se, but we are relying on them. Our samples of food in soup kitchens also get tested. (Masa) So they’re doing their work but you aren't getting the certificate. (Mndeni Mkhize) Part of the problems they are raising, we are in the process of fixing. I think once those structures are there, then we will be able to be issued with those particular certificates. (Masa) So it appears the soup kitchens aren’t legally compliant, but the municipality gives us access to pre-selected sites. (Masa) So we’re at one of the soup kitchens that the municipality insisted that we come see. (Masa) They’re not the sites we wanted to see but municipal officials have none-the-less arrived in numbers. They decline to answer questions on camera and can’t tell us how much a single meal costs. (Masa) Then, out of nowhere, there’s shouting from one of the queues. (Community Member) This is rubbish! We are dogs. (Crowd) Hayibo! (Community Member) The government says they’re giving us food, when they give us this? Is it the mayor that’s giving us this s***? Are we that poor? (Masa) While hundreds of millions are spent to feed the vulnerable, on the ground serious questions remain about what that money is really delivering.

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): When billions are budgeted to feed the hungry… why are children still starving?
metadata.Unique Selling Point: A government feeding scheme where it's unclear exactly where the food is and...who is really being fed.
metadata.Summary: KwaZulu-Natal frequently records the highest number of child deaths due to malnutrition in the country.Recent Mortality Rates: Between April 2017 and April 2025, 555 children under the age of five died from moderate acute malnutrition in KZN public health facilities. In the province, government is spending hundreds of millions to feed the poor. But on the ground, the food being served is raising serious questions. At the centre of our investigation is eThekwini’s soup kitchen programme — a system meant to feed thousands daily. Officially, the municipality says it’s spending around R141 million. But internal documents point to a R240 million figure
metadata.Further information: And when we look closer at how that money is being spent — the numbers don’t add up. In one case, a 10kg bag of samp is priced at R2000 — far above market value. Suppliers are paid through a complex panel system, where multiple companies are appointed, but exactly who supplies what — and at what cost — is difficult to trace. Among them: companies with overlapping directorships… and others, like Msila Media, whose core bu siness - on the surface - appears far removed from feeding communities. But this isn’t just about one programme. Across the province, the cracks are widening. In early childhood development centres — funded through a national budget of over R10 billion — delays in subsidy payments have forced some centres to scale back meals or shut their doors altogether. ECD centres have been forced to take the KZN government to court. And in the school system, a R2.9 billion nutrition tender — feeding more than 2 million learners — is now facing legal challenges, with losing bidders alleging irregularities, newly registered companies being awarded contracts, and claims of political interference. The department denies wrongdoing. But the questions remain. From ECD centres… to school feeding schemes… to municipal soup kitchens — billions are being spent in the name of fighting hunger. And when the system meant to feed the most vulnerable begins to falter… It’s not budgets that suffer. It’s people - it’s children. Hot Soup is an investigation into how a system designed to feed the hungry may be failing them — and what that failure looks like on the ground. 1. Interview: Lawrence Mngomezulu - Deputy Director of Friends of South Africa ECD Forum Mngomezulu is the Deputy Chairperson of the Friends of South Africa Early Childhood Development (ECD) Forum and also runs his own ECD centre in KwaZulu-Natal. The dual role is key: He is both an advocate at provincial level And a practitioner on the ground, dealing directly with children and families The Friends of South Africa ECD Forum is a network representing early childhood development centres across KwaZulu-Natal. nTheir work focuses on especially in low-income communities. Advocating for government subsidies and funding ensuring young children receive: daily meals, etc. They sit at the frontline of child nutrition in poor communities Recent developments in KZN show exactly many ECD centres have not been paid government subsidies on time. Some are owed months — even up to a year — of funding. Mngomezulu provides the “big picture” voice. He can explain: why hunger in KZN is so widespread how food insecurity affects children before they even reach school how fragile the feeding system really is Potential intro: At the very start of a child’s life, before school, before formal systems — early childhood centres are often the first line of defence against hunger. But according to Lawrence Mngomezulu from the Friends of South Africa ECD Forum, even that first line is beginning to crack. Valuable for: scale impact human reality Key questions for him: What are you seeing in terms of hunger among young children in KZN? How dependent are children on meals provided at ECD centres? What happens when subsidies don’t come through? Are more children arriving hungry than before? Are some families dependent on soup kitchens? Interview 2: Family with young children (and Gogo) - areas Chatsworth, Burlington and Moriah Soup kitchens operate between 10 a.m - 2 p.m on the ground Councillor Rowena Bosman is canvassing Mount Moriah for families today. Councillor Samantha Windvogel is canvassing Burlington Founder Dawn Lappan - Thousand Hills says they’ll revert tomorrow with information on potential families we can screen (Outer Western Durban,, 30-40 kms out) Renette Roskruge of Thabitha Foundation says she has families who would be more than willing to interview runs her soup kitchen on Thursday and Friday and will see what she can secure Interview 3: EThekwini Municipality - to be informed of officials name. Committed to:- Sit-down interview Site visits of soup kitchens which we’ll select most problematic based on councillor on the-ground information Two targeted companies: Msila Media Owned by Makhosazane Jennifer Sithole is listed at an RDP home which could very well be her family home - no problem Thing is Makhosazane appears to have dropped from the sky like a hot potato - registering Msila Media in 2020 but with no traceable work or business history before then. How did the 50+ woman survive - perhaps she was a housewife. That’s plausible but perhaps she’s a domestic worker being used as a front but worse of all it’s Makhosazane’s company which lists 10kgs of samp for R 2000 - how did such bizarre pricing pass the eye of the municipality’s precise needle? What’s we’ll do - Claire on the investigative trail - visit the home. Gve her a call and ask her where she operates her business rom but most importantly where she purchases her unique brand of samp for R 2000 for 10kgs. Mavulizibusiso Enterprises/Davport Trading The former lists two directors: Palesa Gwala and Nombuso Nkosingiphile Mcanyana. Mcanyana does not sit in isolation—she is also a director of a second company, Zielungile. Within Zielungile sits Zilungile Portia Nombelana, who is not just a linked name but the owner of Davport Trading. That places Mcanyana and Nombelana one degree apart through a shared company structure. Davport Trading, in turn, appears on the same tender award documentation as Mavulizibusiso Enterprises, bringing the two companies into the same procurement space. The overlap tightens further at a physical level: both Mavulizibusiso Enterprises and Davport Trading list the identical legal address—Umlazi Lodge, Block 23, Room 23, KwaZulu-Natal, 4066. One address, two companies, one tender environment, and a chain of directors that connects them step by step: Mcanyana links Mavulizibusiso to Zielungile; Zielungile links to Nombelana; Nombelana leads to Davport. Shoot dates: 20th and 21st April Presenter: Claire Mawisa
